title: Institute Overview
text: 한국어 English White & NRL Black & Yellow Search the website   SNU Robotics Institute Seoul National University  About › Overview  Institute Overview   At a Glance Director’s Message Vision History Directions  Our Purpose Robotics that begins with people The SNU Robotics Institute brings researchers and laboratories together across disciplines to address the challenges of robotics. We study robots that serve people in care, everyday life, manufacturing and medicine, considering safety, trust, dignity and social acceptance alongside technical performance. Our Approach Intelligence in the body. Cooperation across modules. For robots to act flexibly in the real world, body structure, materials, sensing and control must work together. We investigate embodied physical intelligence arising from interactions between the body and its surroundings, alongside distributed intelligence through cooperation among functional modules. Our aim goes beyond reproducing human form to explore forms and functions that meet human needs. Our Research Four Technical Cores × Three Project Groups Four Technical Cores—MORPHI, MOSAIC, Digital Twin and Human Value—advance shared foundations and approaches to validation. Three Project Groups focus on Life Companion, Wearable and Intra-body robotics, beginning with human needs and practical challenges. Collaboration across TCs and PGs connects foundational technology with application-driven research. Our Community A community that works across disciplines Participating and affiliated faculty connect expertise across engineering, AI, medicine, life sciences and other fields. Researchers can contribute to multiple TCs and PGs, sharing questions and experience while building collaboration across laboratories. Our Impact From research to the real world We work to carry research beyond papers into education, testing in real settings, industry collaboration and technology transfer. We aim to create an environment where students and early-career researchers learn by building and testing, and where researchers and partners explore what robotics can achieve in practice. title: Vision
text: 한국어 English White & NRL Black & Yellow Search the website   SNU Robotics Institute Seoul National University  About › Vision  Vision   At a Glance Director’s Message Vision History Directions  A robotics ecosystem connecting education, research and entrepreneurship SNU Robotics Institute aims to bring together research expertise across disciplines and build an ecosystem in which education and research lead to practical technology applications and new ventures. Through this approach, we seek to become an internationally competitive research institute and strengthen the competitiveness of Korea’s robotics industry. Creative technologies through interdisciplinary research We foster a research environment in which researchers from different fields define and solve problems together. By combining knowledge and research methods across departments and disciplines, we develop robotics technologies that would be difficult to achieve within a single field. Technology innovation driven by societal needs We pursue technologies that address real needs in society and industry. The requirements of users and application environments inform research planning, and the usefulness of new technologies is validated in the field. This process helps research outcomes translate into practical applications. Developing talent through hands-on education We establish an educational foundation that enables students to design, build and experiment directly. Research equipment, spaces and expertise are connected with education to give students experience in solving real problems. We aim to develop robotics talent with both theoretical knowledge and practical implementation skills. Support from technology development to commercialization and entrepreneurship We are building a Lab to Market framework that provides continuous support for technology development, scale-up and commercialization. Technical staff help advance technologies toward commercial use, while market experts and entrepreneurs identify application markets and business opportunities. Our aim is to connect the development of research technologies with preparations for launching new ventures. A research environment that supports continued experimentation and new ventures We envision a “Return to RI” support framework that enables researchers to return to the Institute after pursuing entrepreneurship and continue with further research and new initiatives. We aim to reduce the risks of entrepreneurship and bring experience gained in the field back into research and education.

title: Creative Engineering Design
text: 한국어 English White & NRL Black & Yellow Search the website   SNU Robotics Institute Seoul National University  Education › Creative Engineering Design  Education   Creative Engineering Design Creative Engineering Design Program details and schedules will be announced here.  Developing talent through hands-on education SNU Robotics Institute pursues hands-on education in which students design, build and test robots themselves. We connect research equipment, spaces and the expertise of our researchers to teaching, so that students gain experience solving real problems. Through Creative Engineering Design and the Talent Development Program, we develop robotics talent with both theoretical understanding and the ability to build, and we aim for an ecosystem in which the outcomes of education carry through to research and entrepreneurship.   Creative Engineering Design  Creative Engineering Design is a project-based course in which first-year students in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at Seoul National University work in teams to design and build their own robots. First introduced in 1993 by the late Professor Chong Nam Chu, it has continued for more than 30 years and has become a signature engineering course at the SNU College of Engineering.   About the Course  Students conceive robots that carry out a given mission, then build and test them within limited conditions to solve the problem. Along the way, they develop creativity, teamwork and engineering problem-solving skills. The course content has changed steadily to reflect advances in technology, and since 2024 it has used remote-control devices as a foundation for teaching AI robot architecture.    Curriculum    Creative Engineering Design 1  Computer-aided design and software fundamentals    Creative Engineering Design 2  Robot hardware, motor control, basic circuits and building a working robot      SNU Robocon  The course culminates in Robocon, a team competition in which every student competes with the robot they built in class.    1993  First Creative Engineering Design robot competition    2022  30th anniversary of Creative Engineering Design and the 30th Robocon (Haedong Idea Factory). Winner: Team Zero; runner-up: Team Emergency Rescue; Engineering Award: Team-3; Creativity Award: Team Triple S    2024  The 32nd Robocon, held at the Haedong Advanced Engineering Building as Part 2 of SNU Robotics Day, with 60 students taking part. The winning team, “Jorip-wang” (Assembly King), earned a place in an international Robocon competition.      Student Voices    “Whenever we had an idea, we tested it, and we built our final robot from the ones that worked. When we won, I thought of everything we had been through and couldn’t hold back my tears.”  Team Zero, winner of the 30th Robocon    “We missed the title amid real-world variables, but even if we could turn back time, we couldn’t have done better. We gave it everything.”  Team Emergency Rescue, runner-up of the 30th Robocon    “Determined to win the Robocon game, we stuck together all semester and lived with the rulebook. Because we were always thinking about winning, we had more ideas than we could use.”  Team-3, semifinalist of the 30th Robocon      This course aims to develop a sense of design and creativity by having students design and fabricate various objects through hands-on practice with Internet of Things (IoT) technology, which is widely used across industrial devices and home appliances including automobiles, robots, and smartphones. Building on this foundation, the course further extends to the implementation of Physical AI—artificial intelligence that perceives, reasons about, and acts upon the real world on its own. By utilizing microcontrollers (Arduino, 32-bit MCUs, etc.), students understand the basic structure of an MCU, collect data through various sensors such as temperature, humidity, light, sound, motion, and image, and learn the principles of connecting and controlling output devices such as displays and motors. On this basis, students connect objects through wired and wireless communication and implement on-device AI (TinyML), which learns and infers directly on the device, thereby completing the entire process—from sensing to reasoning and action—as a single integrated system. The course is structured so that students with little experience in coding or hardware can learn step by step from the introductory stage, and by combining theory with hands-on practice, it connects with other engineering design courses, from the fundamentals through to prototype development. This course aims to develop a basic sense of design and fabrication, as well as creativity, through hands-on design and fabrication of a variety of given targets. Intended for first-year students who have not yet formed a clear concept of engineering, it has students build products themselves from specified materials and compete with them, so that they can experience the meaning of engineering with genuine interest. The products take many forms, such as mechanisms and structures, that together reflect the characteristics of various engineering fields. During the first six weeks, lectures on basic design principles, kinematics and fabrication methods are combined with robot programming practice and fabrication. The course consists of two hours of lecture and two hours of lab each week. In week 7, the purpose and rules of the robots that students will design and build are announced, and in week 12 the main competition is held with the robots each team has freely designed and built within the given rules, using the materials and tools provided.

TC 01 · MORPHI BODY Adaptive Robot Materials, Structures and Physical Intelligence Why it matters Robots that move in contact with people must respond safely to unpredictable changes. Handling every response through sensors and complex control algorithms increases computation and energy demand. Materials and structures that distribute forces and adapt mechanically to their surroundings can help overcome the limitations of a fixed robot body. Research approach MORPHI Body combines physical intelligence with structures that change shape and stiffness. Mechanisms are designed to find balance and distribute forces, allowing the body itself to perform part of the computation and control. We also study how robots sense their own physical state and respond to bodily changes, aiming for safe interaction and affordable, energy-efficient hardware. Key research topics Reconfigurable actuation and structures: joints with actively adjustable shape and stiffness, and bio-inspired artificial muscles Self-sensing skin: soft distributed tactile sensors and systems for monitoring the robot’s physical state Modularity and reliability: shared specifications and durability and reliability evaluation for low-cost, low-power hardware Leaders Cho, Kyu-jin Leader Co-leaders Han, Kyung Won Co-leader View researchers 19 Participating Faculty 14 Kang, Ji Heong Dept. of Chemistry Ko, Seung Hwan Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Kim, Jinsoo Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Kim, Ho-young Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Park, Yong-lae Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Yang, Jinkyu Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Lee, Howon Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Jung, Gyuweon School of Transdisciplinary Innovations Cho, Kyu-jin Leader Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Ha, Jung-ik Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Han, Kyung Won Co-leader Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Han, Bohyung Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Hong, Yongtaek Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Sun, Jeong-yun Dept. of Materials Science and Engineering Affiliated Faculty 5 Kim, Taeyong Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Park, Seongjun School of Transdisciplinary Innovations Ahn, Sung-hoon Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Yu, Youngjae School of Transdisciplinary Innovations Yoon, Tae-young Dept. of Biological Sciences  TC 02 · MOSAIC INTELLIGENCE Cooperative Distributed Intelligence and Continual Learning Why it matters Retraining an entire intelligence system whenever a robot’s body or task environment changes demands substantial time and computing resources. Real-world interaction also requires immediate responses to contact and changing conditions. Robots therefore need an architecture that can learn and reconfigure individual functions while coordinating overall behavior. Research approach Inspired by functional specialization and coordination in the brain, MOSAIC Intelligence organizes local intelligence modules under a contextual global intelligence. Local modules learn physical interactions and movement, while global intelligence interprets situations and goals and coordinates their cooperation. We study module recomposition and continual learning across both levels to enable efficient adaptation to different bodies and tasks. Existing digital twins can be fragmented by phenomenon, or face a trade-off between prediction accuracy and computing speed. Faster robot design, learning and validation require accurate, rapid simulation alongside consistent management of diverse data. Research approach The Robot–Human–Environment Digital Twin connects multiphysics simulation, a data fabric and integrated software–hardware optimization. We study how to generate and augment physically consistent data in virtual experiments and connect it with real-world observations for iterative robot design and validation. The aim is an integrated framework that supports everyday assistance, wearable and in-body robotics under their different operating conditions. Robots that directly affect people’s bodies and daily lives must account for human values, including safety, functioning and autonomy. Rather than relying only on ethics or user evaluations after development, these values need to inform design, control and real-world validation from the outset. Research approach Human Value studies a Value Operating System (Value OS) that translates human-centered values into design decisions and control principles that can be verified throughout development. Scenarios reflecting clinical and social contexts are used to examine robot behavior and risks to human values, with findings fed back into subsequent designs. This supports consistent assessment of clinical reliability and social acceptance. title: TC 1 · Adaptive Robot Materials, Structures and Physical Intelligence
text: TC 01 · MORPHI BODY Adaptive Robot Materials, Structures and Physical Intelligence Why it matters Robots that move in contact with people must respond safely to unpredictable changes. Handling every response through sensors and complex control algorithms increases computation and energy demand. Materials and structures that distribute forces and adapt mechanically to their surroundings can help overcome the limitations of a fixed robot body. Research approach MORPHI Body combines physical intelligence with structures that change shape and stiffness. Mechanisms are designed to find balance and distribute forces, allowing the body itself to perform part of the computation and control. We also study how robots sense their own physical state and respond to bodily changes, aiming for safe interaction and affordable, energy-efficient hardware. Key research topics Reconfigurable actuation and structures: joints with actively adjustable shape and stiffness, and bio-inspired artificial muscles Self-sensing skin: soft distributed tactile sensors and systems for monitoring the robot’s physical state Modularity and reliability: shared specifications and durability and reliability evaluation for low-cost, low-power hardware Leaders Cho, Kyu-jin Leader Co-leaders Han, Kyung Won Co-leader View researchers 19 Participating Faculty 14 Kang, Ji Heong Dept. of Chemistry Ko, Seung Hwan Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Kim, Jinsoo Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Kim, Ho-young Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Park, Yong-lae Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Yang, Jinkyu Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Lee, Howon Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Jung, Gyuweon School of Transdisciplinary Innovations Cho, Kyu-jin Leader Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Ha, Jung-ik Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Han, Kyung Won Co-leader Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Han, Bohyung Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Hong, Yongtaek Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Sun, Jeong-yun Dept. of Materials Science and Engineering Affiliated Faculty 5 Kim, Taeyong Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Park, Seongjun School of Transdisciplinary Innovations Ahn, Sung-hoon Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Yu, Youngjae School of Transdisciplinary Innovations Yoon, Tae-young Dept. of Biological Sciences

title: TC 2 · Cooperative Distributed Intelligence and Continual Learning
text: TC 02 · MOSAIC INTELLIGENCE Cooperative Distributed Intelligence and Continual Learning Why it matters Retraining an entire intelligence system whenever a robot’s body or task environment changes demands substantial time and computing resources. Real-world interaction also requires immediate responses to contact and changing conditions. Robots therefore need an architecture that can learn and reconfigure individual functions while coordinating overall behavior. Research approach Inspired by functional specialization and coordination in the brain, MOSAIC Intelligence organizes local intelligence modules under a contextual global intelligence. Local modules learn physical interactions and movement, while global intelligence interprets situations and goals and coordinates their cooperation. We study module recomposition and continual learning across both levels to enable efficient adaptation to different bodies and tasks. Key research topics Autonomous local intelligence: modules that perceive robot–human–environment physical properties and learn movement independently Contextual global intelligence: understanding and predicting situations to coordinate perception and movement modules Continual learning and co-evolution: local and global intelligence learning together and adapting to new environments and missions Leaders Kwak, Nojun Leader Lee, Inah Leader View researchers 29 Participating Faculty 13 Ko, Seung Hwan Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Kwak, Nojun Leader Dept. of Intelligence & Information Kim, Young Min Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Kim, Ju Han College of Medicine Kim, Jinsoo Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Kim, Taesup Graduate School of Data Science Park, Frank C. title: TC 3 · Robot–Human–Environment Digital Twin
text: TC 03 · ROBOT–HUMAN–ENVIRONMENT DIGITAL TWIN Robot–Human–Environment Digital Twin Why it matters Predicting contact between people and robots in changing environments requires multiple physical phenomena to be considered together. Existing digital twins can be fragmented by phenomenon, or face a trade-off between prediction accuracy and computing speed. Faster robot design, learning and validation require accurate, rapid simulation alongside consistent management of diverse data. Research approach The Robot–Human–Environment Digital Twin connects multiphysics simulation, a data fabric and integrated software–hardware optimization. We study how to generate and augment physically consistent data in virtual experiments and connect it with real-world observations for iterative robot design and validation. The aim is an integrated framework that supports everyday assistance, wearable and in-body robotics under their different operating conditions. Key research topics Digital twin: high-accuracy, high-speed simulation of physical interactions and generation of data for learning and validation Data fabric: generating, augmenting, storing and managing large-scale multimodal data while preserving physical consistency and context Infrastructure optimization: integrated software–hardware design for efficient simulation and data processing Leaders Kim, Donyun Leader Co-leaders Jung, Hyungsoo Co-leader View researchers 19 Participating Faculty 11 Kim, Donyun Leader Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Kim, Jinsoo Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Park, Moon Seok College of Medicine (Bundang) Park, Hyungmin Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Ahn, Jooeun Dept. of Physical Education Yang, Jinkyu Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Oh, Joo Hwan Dept. of Mechanical Engineering Won, Jungdam Dept. of Computer Science & Engineering Jung, Hyungsoo Co-leader Graduate School of Data Science Han, Bohyung Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Lee, Jae W. title: TC 4 · Robot Safety, Clinical Reliability and Social Acceptance
text: TC 04 · HUMAN VALUE Robot Safety, Clinical Reliability and Social Acceptance Why it matters Higher performance alone does not make a robot beneficial or trustworthy. Robots that directly affect people’s bodies and daily lives must account for human values, including safety, functioning and autonomy. Rather than relying only on ethics or user evaluations after development, these values need to inform design, control and real-world validation from the outset. Research approach Human Value studies a Value Operating System (Value OS) that translates human-centered values into design decisions and control principles that can be verified throughout development. Scenarios reflecting clinical and social contexts are used to examine robot behavior and risks to human values, with findings fed back into subsequent designs. This supports consistent assessment of clinical reliability and social acceptance. Key research topics Value-based design: defining indicators for safety, functioning and autonomy and using them in design and validation Demonstration and stress testing: identifying thresholds of value compromise across interaction scenarios and explaining assessment results Shared criteria and design feedback: studying a Human Value API and trust criteria, and feeding evaluation results into control and design improvements Leaders Kim, Hongsoo Leader Co-leaders Park, Hyunwoo Co-leader View researchers 19 Participating Faculty 12 Kim, Kee Won College of Medicine Kim, Young Min Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Kim, Hyeoneui College of Nursing Kim, Hongsoo Leader Graduate School of Public Health Park, Juyeon Dept. of Textiles, Merchandising & Fashion Design Park, Hyunwoo Co-leader Graduate School of Data Science Baek, Sung Hee Dept. of Biological Sciences Seo, Jongmo Dept. of Electrical & Computer Engineering Yoon, Chang Hwan College of Medicine (Bundang) Lee, Joonhwan Dept. of Communication Jeong, Chang Wook College of Medicine Jo, Yohan Graduate School of Data Science Affiliated Faculty 7 Ro, Du Hyun College of Medicine Mook-Jung, Inhee College of Medicine Park, Myungwoo College of Medicine (Boramae) Park, Sangchul School of Law Beom, Jaewon College of Medicine (Bundang) Ahn, Woo-young Dept. of Psychology Lee, Soo-hyun Dept. of Psychology
